content.thinking:
I'm planning a frost-forged League of Legends style battle axe, deciding to display it upright on a stand with the butt spike embedded in a base, sized to realistic axe proportions around 1.1 meters.

I'm sketching the asymmetric double-bit design, with a large crescent blade on one side and a smaller ice-crystal spike cluster on the other, oriented in the XY plane for a readable front profile, keeping the construction simple to minimize API risk since I won't be testing.

I need a single root joint since the rig requires at least one, so I'll place a root joint named "axe" at the origin, with all parts defaulting to it since no moving parts are needed. For the base, I'm planning a hexagonal plinth around 0.28m radius and 0.1m tall in dark stone with an icy rim, supporting a haft roughly 1.2m tall so the whole piece stands about 1.5m total.

Scaling it out more concretely: plinth height 0.16m, haft running from y=0.16 to 1.30, blades centered near y=1.05, and a spike tip reaching y=1.55 for a total height around 1.55m -- vertical rather than tilted to keep the floor contact simple. I'm defining the plinth as a lathe shape using an octagonal profile (8 segments) with an outline that sweeps out from the axis and back to form the tiered stone base, sitting flush with y=0 for floor contact.

For the color palette I'm settling on a frosty League-style scheme: icy cyan glow, pale white highlights, deep indigo/navy steel body, and a warm gold trim accent for contrast, keeping total flat colors well under the limit. I'm planning to use the cel-paint toon kit so the blade face reads with a bright icy edge, mid-blue body, and darker fuller grooves, and I'm now working out the local outline coordinates needed to extrude that blade shape.

Now I'm sketching the actual polygon points for a crescent bearded axe blade — socket near the haft around x=0.04, sweeping horn tip near x=0.32-0.46, with the outer cutting edge bulging outward to form a convex "D"-like curve, trying to make sure the points stay non-self-intersecting.

This gives horns pointing up and down near x=0.27 with the outer edge bulging to 0.49, forming more of a convex kite than a hooked crescent — the edges aren't concave between tips. I think this is really shaping up to be a double-wide, bearded, butterfly-like blade rather than a true hooked crescent.

Still plotting the crescent curve points...

Capping bevel at half thickness to avoid issues with sharp concave corners, I'm rethinking the blade construction as layered pieces: a darker steel body with a small bevel, plus a separate lighter inner face to suggest a cutting edge, rather than relying on a single tapered extrude.

I'll make this icy white-cyan edge glint a thin outer outline layer, then add a scaled-down inset "blue steel" layer centered within it to read as a beveled edge, with decals on top. Scaling the inset uniformly about the blade's centroid keeps it safely non-self-intersecting even with the star-like horn tips.

For the glowing frost-core, I'm considering a third inset layer scaled further in and tinted emissive cyan, but I think a textured plane decal carrying fine rune/frostfern linework would read better than a simple geometric inset -- using transparency so only the glowing lines show against the blade face.

Working out the front and back plane placement now: I need both planes positioned at the blade's front and back surfaces with correct orientation so the texture reads unmirrored from each viewing direction, matching the convention that a viewer facing the model sees +X on their right.

For the head shape, I'm planning a symmetrical double-bit design: the main crescent blade on +X side, and a smaller mirrored counter-blade on -X side scaled down, being careful that mirroring with the x-axis flip doesn't invert the thickness direction incorrectly.

I'm reconsidering the back side design—leaning toward a smaller bearded blade paired with an icy crystal spike cluster for a more exaggerated, stylized look, plus a crystalline hex-prism ice spear spike mounted on a socket at the top, and a butt spike at the bottom into the plinth. Now I'm working out the haft's vertical stacking from the plinth top up through the head center to the top spike.

I'm shaping the haft as an octagonal rod with a realistic 4.4cm diameter, going for a frost-forged ironwood look wrapped in leather and silver rings, applying a painted wood-grain texture via a cel-shaded paint layer, and tuning the radius so it reads clearly. I'm also estimating total painted surface area across the haft and blades to gauge texture density for baking.

Working out the paint sheet resolution, I land on 1024px as a good balance giving roughly 1.4mm texels, sufficient for the rim lines and bands on the blades without needing a heavier 2048 atlas. For the blade's inset body layer, I'm defining a gradient paint that shifts from deep blue near the haft to cyan at the edge based on distance from centroid, distinguishing faces from edge walls by normal direction, and letting the cel-shading's directional light naturally light the front face while shadowing the back for a stylized look.

Checking how the cel-shading paint resolves nested paints — making sure the shadow calculation correctly uses the current surface coordinate when resolving a lit paint without explicit position, by passing it through the enclosing paint call's context. Now I'm sketching the steel-blue gradient colors for the blade's front face, moving from a dark navy near the haft through a mid blue to a lighter tone near the edge.

Writing blade paint function...

Adding thin lighter-blue stripe highlights where noise thresholds hit, then handling wall-facing normals with a bright ice-edge color so layer boundaries stay visible.

For the outer layer, I'm giving it a flat pale rim color so it reads as a thin edge frame around the thicker inner layer, with rim width varying unevenly based on distance from centroid—wider at horn tips, thinner near center.

Simplifying the color layering: skipping the ink backing idea, I'll keep A as pale cyan paint and let B sit visibly on top since it's thinner and smaller, creating a natural bevel edge. I'm adding a third glowing crescent inlay layer, inset further with its own thickness for a cyan glow accent.

Actually, I'll simplify to a hexagonal frost gem embedded in a metal ring boss on each blade face, using a low-poly cylinder for the gem shape with a glowing cyan material, plus a decorative rune decal etched along the blade surface.

Now I'm mapping the decal drawing coordinates onto the plane geometry, converting model-space positions to SVG units with a viewBox scaled around 90x234, then planning stroke widths relative to the raster output size so the filigree lines render crisply at 640px.

Still sketching the frost fern and filigree paths..., then checking color treatment — cyan glow with a white core — and positioning the decal plane just off the blade's front face so it doesn't poke through the silhouette.

Now I'm moving to the haft construction: adding metal langets running down from the head, then blocking out the eye/socket as a lathed octagonal barrel shape that the blade head attaches to.

I'm now working out the overall proportions, deciding how tall the socket, spike, and haft should be relative to each other so the final head doesn't end up too tall or short — aiming for the head center around 0.86-0.88 with the spike adding roughly 0.3 on top.

Realizing the blade span is too exaggerated at over a meter tall, I'm deciding to scale the whole blade outline down by a factor of 0.8 to bring the proportions back toward something more balanced while keeping the stylized look.

Now I'm plotting the raw outline points for the blade before scaling, tracing the inner boundary up to the upper horn tip and then around the outer edge, making sure the path doesn't self-intersect.

Continuing down the outline, I'm checking convexity around the lower horn and considering adding small jagged "teeth" to the outer edge near point 7 to give the shape more icy character.

I'll scale the inset piece by about 0.8 around its centroid and work out the reach and vertical span for a smaller back blade, which I can flip across the x-axis to mirror-place it.

The back blade will skip the rune decal and instead get a gem accent with a small crescent plus icy crystal cluster. For the top, I'm shaping a spearhead as a leaf-like outline extruded flat so it reads clearly from the front, giving it thin thickness for a crystalline look.

I'm adding a second thinner extrude rotated 90 degrees to form a cross-blade spike, colored icy with a glowing core. Below, I'm planning the haft's ferrule and spike embedding into a tiered plinth with octagonal base layers and a frozen ice mound of crystals clustered near the bottom.

Now I'm scattering icicle spikes radially around the haft base using hexagonal-section geometry, giving the biggest ones a glow. For the plinth itself, I'm painting the top faces frosty white-cyan with noise while keeping the sides dark slate with cracked patches, blending the two based on surface normal direction.

I also want to add an engraved rune ring on the plinth's top face — a glowing circular decal with tick marks and glyphs — though I need to make sure it doesn't get obscured by the haft above it.

Working out the plinth's lathe profile now, stacking octagonal tiers with chamfered steps to build up the radius and height.

I'm also thinking about adding decorative gem studs around the octagonal tier 2 faces, placing small glowing octahedra at the vertex angles so they sit centered on the sides rather than floating between them.

Either placement works, so I'll settle on the gem as a small octahedron near the stud's edge radius. Now I'm mapping out the haft structure from bottom to top: a ferrule spike embedded in the head, a dark wood shaft with grain texture, and silver bands marking the collar, grip transition, and mid-shaft points.

Writing leather wrap spiral stripe logic...

Still defining ferrule geometry...

Then I'll leave bare wood from 0.305–0.50, leather grip from 0.50–0.80, and continue wood up to the head centered around y=0.92, sizing the socket region to match the scaled blade's inner boundary so the horns extend beyond it.

Checking that the blade body still touches the socket radius confirms the connection is solid. Now I'm placing the lower langets as thin flat straps running down the haft from the socket, defining their box dimensions and position using frustumBox with width along x and depth along z.

Writing langet outline...

Still shaping the socket profile...

Still refining bracket coordinates...

The blade boundary extends up at that point, so the bracket sits comfortably within the interior with proper clearance over the B shape. I'll handle the lower bracket by mirroring the y-coordinates of the same point set, which should work regardless of winding order. Now I need to check the gem boss position along the x-axis.

Positioning the silver boss ring and gem now — a lathed ring profile with a faceted octahedron gem glowing cyan, placed on the front face and scaled for a pointed look.

I'm defining a helper function to simplify positioning coordinates relative to the head's vertical offset. Beyond that, I'm planning additional details like icicle shards bursting from the back of the head, hanging icicles under the blade horns, and a tattered frost-blue cloth tassel dangling from the socket.

For the tassel, I decide on a simple pennant shape extruded flat in the XY plane in front of the haft, with a swallowtail cut, hanging below the socket front with painted rune patterns on its face.

Refining the swallowtail taper and placement near the haft, I'm positioning the pennant slightly offset from the haft front with a small gap, and adding a gold ring cinched around the haft just below the socket to attach it.

I move the pennant start lower to avoid overlapping the socket's flare, then plan a separate gold ring-tie lathed around the haft with a radius narrowing from 0.026 to 0.034. I check that the langets' x and z ranges don't collide with the pennant's position, confirm they don't, and decide to keep the langets for visual richness before moving on to planning the ice crystal clusters.

I'm now setting up a ring of nine spiky plinth bases around the haft, varying angle, radius, tilt, length, and section, cycling through a few flat icy colors. I also plan frost thorn spikes jutting from the socket and blade roots at the back of the head.

I'm sketching additional icicle shards sprouting along the blade's edge near the horn junction, plus small crystal clusters embedded at the gem root on both faces, each with hand-specified positions and outward directions using the hexagonal spike section helper.

I'm also considering a hanging icicle drip off the lower horn tip, pointing straight down with a tapered point, checking whether it floats properly or needs adjusting to embed into the horn geometry.

For the back of the design, I'm planning a smaller mirrored blade at reduced scale, inset around its centroid, skipping the gold bracket and giving it a small gem instead, plus a few icy thorn spikes clustered near the socket root for extra decoration.

I'm also considering adding frost-fern card elements standing upright on the plinth top—flat quads with jagged crystalline SVG textures, cross-arranged and spun for variety, facing upward so lighting hits them brightly, avoiding anything that floats off-model.

Now I'm setting up the module imports needed for the build: THREE, geometry merging utilities, the builder, frame, and other shared helpers, being careful to only import what's actually used since unused imports will fail typecheck. I'm starting to write the import statements and type declarations...

I'm thinking through whether to use INK as the color for a cartoon-style outline layer sitting behind the main blade shape — essentially an ink silhouette scaled up slightly from the centroid and placed underneath the main geometry at a thinner stroke width than the primary outline.

I'll settle on a plum-black ink tone for the main blade, applied cheaply since all blades share the function, while frame imports handle card frames and rng handles cards and crystals. Now I'm writing a helper to scale outline points by a factor while preserving sharp corner markers.

Writing scaling and raw blade data...

Still defining blade layers...

Still writing shader colors...

Checking the lighting logic, I realize the back face normal always points away from the key light, so it would render fully in shadow tone -- a bit flat, so I'm considering a separate paint rule for the back to add some variation.

Still writing lighting helpers...

Thinking further, flat faces facing both directions would always register as lit, so the painted gradient alone handles shading there, while cel-based variation stays reserved for non-planar geometry like bevels.

Since the engine uses standard materials with real lighting anyway, the cel palette is just a baked-in accent, so I'm deciding to skip it for blades entirely and reserve it for cylinders and lathed parts to keep things consistent. Now I'm defining the core color palette—deep blues, icy whites, cyan glow, and gold tones—for the different material layers.

Setting up cel-shaded variants for gold, steel, and dark steel, plus a cool blue-toned wood grain pattern and leather striping. I'm also confirming that cel shading can wrap around a grain paint object, and thinking through how to add an engraved gold line detail on the socket using height-banded paint logic.

Now I'm working out the rivet geometry—merging small spheres into a single part per color group so they share attributes, then placing them in a ring around the socket joint using translation and a loop. I'm also deciding to keep gold as a flat color string rather than a cel paint to limit the total color count, since painted pieces don't add to that budget.

Switching to the blade decal, I'm mapping the SVG viewBox coordinates to the physical blade region so runes and the gem align correctly—working out the scale factor (250 units per meter), converting key points like the gem center and ornament edges into SVG space, and making sure nothing exceeds the blade's bounding inset.

Now I'm sketching the interior decal lines, starting with a curved edge-guard arc that traces just inside the blade's outer silhouette.

Still mapping the boundary curve...

Still writing path layering code...

Now I need to work out orientation for the back decal: since the plane faces -Z, a viewer standing behind looking toward +Z sees +X to their left, so I need to map the SVG's horizontal axis onto -X to keep the design readable from that side.

Actually simpler to generate a mirrored version via an SVG group transform rather than fighting plane orientation, so I'll write a `runes(mirror)` function that flips the drawing for the back face. For the small blade decal, I'll skip the runes and just place a gem plus a gold stud, scaling and repositioning the decal for the mirrored -X side.

Scaling thickness for the small blade by a factor, then defining a blade-building function with parameters for scale, side, and thickness. I'm computing the gem boss position proportionally to the scale factor so it stays correctly placed on each blade, then setting up the lathe-generated ring profile scaled the same way.

Writing blade function code...

Both faces share the same scale, so painting stays consistent. I'm adding gold brackets to both blades using a scaled version of the bracket outline, mirrored for the opposite side, and now considering a thin glowing cyan vein along the cutting edge using a swept path through the outer boundary points.

Still planning the sweep...

I'm deciding to drop the redundant first curve from the decal, keeping just the second curve plus the glowing edge strip, then starting to work out the lathe geometry for the spear's top socket.

Now I'm defining the spear blade shape as two crossed leaf profiles extruded with a slight bevel, positioned to sit just inside the socket's top radius so the tip lands around 1.55 units up with a socket height of 0.92.

For coloring, I'm planning a pale cyan gradient along the spear's length based on local coordinates, and considering adding a smaller inset glowing core shape at half scale to give the blade a bright crystalline center.

Now I'm defining the haft: a vertical octagonal wooden rod from near the base up to the top of the hornspan, using the rod builder with a small radius and wood paint for flat beveled faces.

Then I add a leather-wrapped grip section as a separate thinner rod, and a helper function for metal bands that lathes a small ring profile around the haft at a given height, with slightly inset inner edges so it reads as a solid cylindrical collar.

I'm placing several bands along the haft at varying heights with gold and steel coloring, plus leather accent rings near the ends, and then designing the pommel ferrule as a lathed profile sinking slightly into the plinth, built from a sequence of radius/height points to get a stepped, flanged shape with a gold accent ring to follow.

Now I'm skipping the ferrule fins and moving to the langets—flat extruded shapes positioned symmetrically on either side of the haft, with a pointed bottom tip and beveled edges in a light steel tone, plus small rivet spheres studding them in pairs along their length, finished in gold.

Checking the haft radius against the langet placement so the inner faces sit flush against the octagonal shaft, then positioning the pennant above and slightly forward so its depth range clears the langets without collision. I'm now defining the pennant's cloth pattern—a blue gradient base with gold trim along the edges and top, and a white chevron zigzag motif near the bottom.

Realizing the pennant currently overlaps and hides the leather grip section, so I need to shorten its hanging length and redraw its swallowtail outline with adjusted vertex coordinates to avoid that overlap while keeping the polygon non-self-intersecting.

I'm also adding a small gold tie-ring band near the top of the haft where the pennant attaches, and sketching out a rune-disc decal texture for the plinth top with concentric cyan rings, tick marks, and glyph-like arrow symbols between them.

For the frost decal, I'm placing a circular plane sized to match the plinth tier's top face, offsetting it slightly in z to avoid flickering against the surface. I'm skipping separate side decals for the plinth and instead planning small glowing octahedron gems as studs at the tier-2 vertices.

Now for painting the plinth itself: I'll use a mottled white/frost texture on upward-facing surfaces, a patchwork of dark blue tones on the sides using a patch-based pattern, and an icy blue dusting on the mid-slope normals to simulate snow accumulation.

Then I want to add inner white lines to the frost shapes and figure out card placement - clustering them near the haft base at smaller radius rather than over the rune disc, and considering the tier-1 ledge as another spot.

Finishing the card parameters with random spin and slight bend, keeping default white tint since the texture carries its own colors. Now I'm thinking about adding larger crystal spikes.

Writing spike placement code...

Still placing crystals...

Adding a secondary small spike near the small blade horn, and reconsidering whether extra hanging icicles are needed along the bottom edge — deciding to skip that since the edge isn't horizontal. I'm also thinking about adding small gold rivet spheres at the bracket points on each blade, roughly four per blade near their centers.

Placing rivets at the computed centers and mirroring the lower bracket vertically to preserve the sharp tip. These bracket coordinates are already scaled for the main blade, so I'll apply the ratio r to match the smaller blade, then move on to the boss lathe ring, gem inlays, rune rings, and glow edge strip paths.

Still working out the glow strip geometry...

I should check the lowest point touches the ground plane properly, and keep the silhouette readable from a top-down camera like LoL-style icons. I'm deciding to skip extra engraved gold filigree on the socket to keep part count reasonable, settling on roughly a hundred parts total, with plinth corner gems and inner steel/wood haft details still to add.

Writing rune path data...

I realize the boss ring near the gem overlaps the decal spokes, so I'm shrinking the ring radius to about 15 units and repositioning the spokes to start further out, keeping clearance from the edge.

Checking the gem position against model coordinates confirms it lands at svg (46,125), and I'm adding snowflake dots at a few fixed points plus small notch glyphs tracing along the outline bands.

I'm mirroring the stripe group with a horizontal flip transform, placing the vertical rune stripe near the horn tip, then drafting the plinth runes SVG with concentric circles.

Writing SVG circles...

Writing material paints...

Spear paint gradient blending blue tones by height, and I'm setting up frames for card parts attached to the root joint since literal positions have no bone. I'm estimating around 120 parts total, keeping triangle count reasonable, and making sure colors are always passed in before merging all the geometries together.

Writing merge helper functions...

Still writing lathe profile...

Skipping the frost crystals for now. I need to fix the mirrorY helper's type inference since TS struggles with tuple literals in a ternary — I'll switch to explicit loops pushing typed tuples to avoid the union type issue.

Writing transform helper function...

I'm also reasoning about winding order — mirroring Y flips the loop's winding direction, so I should reverse point order inside mirrorY to keep it consistent for extrusion. Now I'm sketching a scale transform for the back-blade that scales points relative to a center point.

Computing glow strip points by mapping selected blade edge indices through a scaled transform, then setting z per face using a thickness offset for front and back. I verify the catmull spline helper and sweep function signatures match what I need, and plan the octahedron gem part with its own scale.

I'm now sizing the gem and boss ring, checking the octahedron's half-height against the ring's radius so the gem sits properly on top without being swallowed by the ring geometry.

Writing metadata and blade config...

Setting the shard viewBox dimensions so stroke widths render crisply at the chosen scale. I'm defining a crystal helper that wraps the spike primitive with hexagonal cross-sections and optional glow, overloading it to accept either a direction vector or a tip point.

Now I'm lathing the plinth profile with chamfered steps, checking normals along the curve to decide where frost should accumulate based on surface angle, and confirming the bottom rests at y=0 with nothing lower in the scene.

Working out the pennant extrusion placement and sizing, then writing the cloth paint function that colors the gold edges by checking surface normal direction and trimming fabric boundaries using the shape coordinates to mask out the slanted edges and top border.

For the center detail, I'm adding a white diamond and a smaller cyan diamond inside it, blending a base gradient color between two blues based on vertical position. For the blade edges I'll just use a simple flat ice color rather than a shader, keeping unused callback parameters prefixed with underscores, and tallying up my final palette of flat colors.

Now I'm writing the blade paint function, computing coordinates and a cloud noise texture to blend between deep, mid, and ice colors along the blade length, then adding diagonal streak highlights and darker shading near the root...

Checking the lathe signature for the gold ring bands, then moving on to building decal planes for surface details.

I'm positioning the decal planes relative to the ornament's scale, figuring out their center offsets and sizes, and working through how the texture orientation needs to mirror depending on which side (front or back) and direction the piece faces.

Finishing up, I'm double-checking all the imported helpers—grain, mottle, patches, noise, smoothstep, cel, INK, glow, mergeGeometries—are actually used so there's no dead code before writing the final file.

I'm defining a leather paint function that cycles through dark navy, light blue-gray, and medium blue bands based on a phase calculation, then deciding to wrap it with cel shading using the resolve helper for lighting. For the plinth, I'm planning to apply the stone cel shading only to the sides while giving the top a frosted look.

Finalizing the socket and ferrule to use steel cel shading, and laying out the haft bands with alternating gold and steel colors at specific positions along the shaft. I'm matching the band radii to the underlying rod geometry — grip, wood, and band radii all need to line up at the flat faces and vertices — before writing out the final code string, with no extra ground-wear detail needed.
